source first, audit technical SEO/GEO from current evidence, calculate the rolling
Daily Report mix before topic selection, publish exactly one new bilingual Daily
Report, and deliver the public change through one fresh branch and one non-draft

The first complete ten-report window before today's publication is **7
eBPF-centered / 2 pure Agent / 1 adjacent systems**. The oldest item that will
age out is `agent-trace-evidence-budget`, a pure-Agent report. Publishing another
eBPF-centered report today would therefore create an **8 eBPF / 1 Agent / 1
adjacent** window and violate the repository's 5–7 eBPF rule.

The selected question is **whether a GPU profiler can prove which host action
caused a slow kernel in asynchronous CUDA execution**. It uses the approved GPU
and Heterogeneous Runtime Systems queue. eBPF is a strong host evidence source,
but the causal mechanism remains valid with another host tracer and relies
equally on CUPTI and CUDA dependency semantics, so the report is classified as
adjacent systems. After publication the rolling window becomes **7 eBPF / 1 pure
Agent / 2 adjacent out of 10**.

No unrelated technical SEO implementation change is included because current
evidence does not establish a new defect.

## Rolling topic mix and report selection

Current archive before today's report:

- eBPF-centered: **7 of 10**;
- pure Agent: **2 of 10**;
- adjacent systems: **1 of 10**.

The active eBPF Observability and Profiling roadmap was searched first. Its three
preferred remaining questions are semantic compression, application-defined
resource profiling, and GPU causal profiling. The first two are naturally
eBPF-centered in the current roadmap and cannot be published today without
exceeding the eBPF cap after the oldest pure-Agent report ages out.

GPU causal profiling can be asked honestly as an adjacent host/device systems
question. The report does not claim that eBPF is the causal mechanism. Instead,
it treats eBPF as one host evidence source alongside CUPTI's native CUDA
correlation and dependency semantics. This keeps classification faithful to the
technical question and produces a compliant **7 / 1 / 2** rolling window.

Existing material was searched for overlap. The older GPU observability article
identifies the broad cross-layer visibility gap and argues for programmable GPU
instrumentation. The repository also contains CUPTI correlation tutorials. The
new report advances a narrower question that these artifacts do not answer:
**what evidence makes a claimed host-to-kernel causal path testable when streams,
graphs, host queues, identifier reuse, and telemetry loss create ambiguity?**

## Research evidence and novelty gate

Primary or authoritative evidence includes:

- NVIDIA CUPTI Activity API usage and correlation documentation: <https://docs.nvidia.com/cupti/main/main.html>
- NVIDIA CUPTI Activity API reference, including dropped-record accounting and kernel queued/submitted timestamps: <https://docs.nvidia.com/cupti/api/group__CUPTI__ACTIVITY__API.html>
- NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide asynchronous execution, stream ordering, and cross-stream event dependencies: <https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/02-basics/asynchronous-execution.html>
- Linux kernel uprobe tracing documentation: <https://docs.kernel.org/trace/uprobetracer.html>
- Zheng et al., *SysOM-AI: Continuous Cross-Layer Performance Diagnosis for Production AI Training*: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29235>
- Darzi et al., *Host-Side Telemetry for Performance Diagnosis in Cloud and HPC GPU Infrastructure*: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16946>
- Zheng et al., *gpu_ext: Extensible OS Policies for GPUs via eBPF*: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12615>

Current CUPTI documentation establishes several important local mechanisms:
CUDA API calls and resulting kernels/memcpy/memset records can share a
correlation ID; external correlation can connect higher-level IDs to CUDA API
activity; CUDA Graph activity exposes graph/node identity; and kernel records can
carry queued/submitted timestamps when latency timestamps are enabled. CUDA
stream/event semantics establish a partial order that a timestamp-sorted trace
cannot infer reliably.

The report therefore does not claim to invent CUDA correlation. Its gap is the
lack of a durable, lifetime-aware host/device causal identity and an evaluation
that scores causal edge correctness under ambiguous timestamps and missing
records.

Three developed directions are included:

1. a generation-scoped host-device causal token that treats CUPTI correlation IDs as typed local edges rather than a global work identity;
2. a dependency-aware critical-path graph that distinguishes explicit, observed, inferred, and missing edges;
3. an adversarial host/device causality benchmark with ground-truth parent edges and paired cases whose timestamps look similar while true dependencies differ.

The thesis is falsifiable. If framework tracing plus current CUPTI correlation
already reconstructs request-to-kernel critical paths accurately across
multi-threaded, multi-stream, graph-heavy workloads, a new causal namespace is
unnecessary. If timestamp-only stitching matches the typed graph on adversarial
cases, the graph machinery adds little value. If production diagnosis only needs
cohort-level anomaly localization, exact per-operation causality may not justify
its overhead.
